Moeslim Taher (10 September 1934 – 23 November 1999) was an Indonesian educator and co-founder of Universitas Jayabaya, established on 5 October 1958 in Jakarta alongside Yuyun Moeslim Taher through notary act by Liem Toeng Kie. Born in Sigli, Aceh, Taher entered education early, teaching at an elementary school in Padang while attending junior high and later teaching at private secondary schools. He earned a Sarjana Hukum from Universitas Jayabaya in 1965, followed by further degrees including a doctorate from Universitas Padjadjaran in 1979, and served as the university's second rector, expanding its faculties in law, economics, and beyond to promote private higher education in Indonesia.

Richard Sanderson (baptised 4 January 1784 – 28 October 1857) was a British merchant, banker, and Conservative ""Conservative Party (UK)"") and Tory ""Tories (British political party)"") politician.

Born near Doncaster, Yorkshire, Sanderson was the son of Thomas Anderson of Armthorpe and Sarah née Cromack, daughter of John Cromack. In 1833, he married Charlotte Matilda Manners-Sutton, daughter of Charles Manners-Sutton, 1st Viscount Canterbury, and they had at least 10 children — six sons, and four daughters, including Thomas Sanderson, 1st Baron Sanderson.

[edit&action=edit&section=2 ""Edit section: Business career"")] [...] Early in his adult life, Sanderson became a clerk in London bill-broking firm Richardson, Overend, and Company, where the quaker Samuel Gurney ""Samuel Gurney (1786–1856)"") was a partner—which some historians suggest means Sanderson may also have a quaker upbringing. By 1827, Sanderson was operating as a bill broker but at his own business, dominating the London market in the later years of that decade alongside Gurney's business, then renamed Overend, Gurney and Company—both at Lombard Street in London.

In 1837, Sanderson moved his business to King William Street, London; in 1847, that business then had to suspend payment, before being able to trade again in early 1848. [...] Just two weeks after his death in 1857, the business—then known as Sanderson, Sandeman and Company—failed with debts of £5,299,006.

Sanderson first became Member of Parliament (MP) for Colchester ""Colchester (UK Parliament constituency)"") at a by-election in 1829"")—held due to the resignation of Sir George Smyth, 6th Baronet. Having cultivated anti-Catholic and Tory relationships, he was put forward by the Colchester corporation to replace Smyth, a fellow Tory. A ""token challenge"" was put forward to counter Sanderson's bid for the seat, but he won the seat, declaring a desire to promote ""the education of the poor"" and to ""put an end to the traffic in human blood"".

Bernard “went to the first club who was interested”. He accepts that was a “mistake” because he “always wanted to be at Newcastle” and his six months at Southampton were a disaster. A season at Rangers, where he was “shocked” by the standard of Scottish football, was only a slight improvement.

“Then I was on my way to Leeds, to join John Carver (the former, and future, Newcastle coach), when Freddy Shepherd (the Newcastle chairman) called,” Bernard says. “I turned the car around straightaway. It was a dream come true. Well, until it was a nightmare.”

Before he made a senior appearance during his second Newcastle spell, Bernard landed awkwardly in a reserve match and suffered a hip injury. [...] “I fell in love with the north east when I played for Newcastle and I guess I just never really left,” Bernard says, boasting a discernible Gallic twang but pronouncing vowels like a born-and-bred Geordie. “My wife is from here. My kids were born here. This is where I call home now.

“I didn’t expect to be living here 20 years after I first arrived, I’ll admit. Not after my first conversation with Bobby Robson. Everyone may remember me as a left-back for Newcastle, but I was a centre-forward through all my youth. I played up front for France Under-18s with Nicolas Anelka, with Steed Malbranque behind us. [...] Joining Newcastle had been a “fluke”. A friend of Bernard’s agent knew the representative of Didier Domi, a fellow French defender formerly with Newcastle, and it was through him that the trial arrived. He also had a week-long try-out at West Ham United, but Robson offered him a year-long deal, despite Bernard being unable to speak English and communicating in Spanish via Solano.

Lyon withheld Bernard’s international clearance, prevented him from playing until the November, before he was sent on loan to fourth-tier Darlington to “toughen up”. Eventually his opportunity came, initially as a winger — until Robert arrived.

Olivier Bernard has been speaking to BBC Radio Newcastle about how he evolved into an attacking left-back during his time with the Magpies after joining as a forward.

The Frenchman arrived in 2000 aged 20 and spent the next four and a half years of his career at the club, helping Sir Bobby Robson's side to a series of high Premier League finishes and representing Newcastle in European competition.

Dislodging the club's all-time leading goalscorer Alan Shearer was an almost impossible task, but Robson suggested a change of position that led to him becoming a first-team regular. [...] He added: ""I loved it, I was playing in a very attacking team, full of youth and we had pace to burn. It was exciting. Even though it wasn't a position that I would have chosen, I've enjoyed playing at left-back for Newcastle.""
Listen to more from BBC Radio Newcastle's Total Sport on BBC Sounds
Football [...] Now 44, Bernard told BBC Radio Newcastle: ""I was a forward player when I first came to Newcastle. I wanted the number nine shirt but obviously I got denied by Alan!

I played a little bit on the left and then they bought Laurent Robert. I was young, I just wanted to play and the gaffer asked if I wanted to try to play at left-back. I said that as long as I was playing, I would give 100%. That's how I ended up playing at full-back and I learned on the spot.

The good thing was we had the ball more often than not, so I played as an advanced full-back. In that era, Ashley Cole started full-backs going forward and pushing the team to do better things. In the early 2000s, that's when the position of the full-backs changed.""

Olivier’s association with the northeast goes all the way back to 2000 when he joined a Newcastle side managed by Sir Bobby Robson – a man he describes as “probably the best English manager ever.” He soon headed down the road to Darlington on loan – an experience that he calls “the best thing I’ve ever done.” It is clear even from this early stage of our chat that this man is sincerely grateful for the way in which the local community has accepted him over the past fourteen years.

Durham City FC – the Northern League club that he owns – is Bernard’s way of thanking the region. [...] The episode is typical of Bernard’s attitude and loyalty towards Newcastle and the northeast. He is totally committed to creating a link between the club and the University – perhaps even borrowing some players from Team Durham.

When this interview was set up, I didn’t know what to expect. Spending forty minutes with Olivier was an absolute pleasure.
